# Hardy-Lorentz Spaces: Atomic Decomposition, Interpolation, and Operator Theory

## Introduction

This paper is devoted to the study of the Hardy-Lorentz spaces $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ within the parameter ranges $0 < p \le 1$ and $0 < q \le \infty$. These spaces arise naturally at the intersection of classical Hardy space theory and the Lorentz scale of function spaces, providing a refined framework that captures subtle distributional properties beyond those visible in the standard Hardy spaces $H^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. By allowing the second parameter $q$ to vary independently of $p$, the Hardy-Lorentz spaces offer a more delicate calibration of integrability, which proves valuable in a variety of analytic contexts.

## Atomic Decomposition

A central contribution of this work is the development of an atomic decomposition that characterizes the elements belonging to these spaces. Atomic decompositions have long been recognized as one of the most powerful tools in the theory of Hardy spaces, reducing the study of general distributions to the analysis of simple, well-understood building blocks known as atoms. In the present setting, we establish that every element of $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ admits a decomposition into atoms, with the associated coefficients organized in a manner that reflects the Lorentz-space structure. This characterization not only clarifies the internal structure of the Hardy-Lorentz spaces but also furnishes a practical mechanism for verifying membership and for proving boundedness results.

## Interpolation Properties

Building upon the atomic framework, the paper examines the interpolation properties that hold among the Hardy-Lorentz spaces. We investigate how these spaces behave under both real and complex interpolation methods, demonstrating that the family $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ forms a coherent scale under interpolation. These results position the Hardy-Lorentz spaces as natural intermediate spaces and provide effective tools for transferring estimates across different values of the parameters $p$ and $q$.

## Action of Singular Integrals

A significant portion of the analysis is directed toward understanding how singular integral operators behave when acting on functions in these spaces. Singular integrals, including the Calderón-Zygmund operators that are ubiquitous in harmonic analysis and partial differential equations, are studied here with respect to their mapping properties on $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Using the atomic decomposition as a foundational tool, we establish boundedness results that show these operators respect the Hardy-Lorentz structure, thereby extending classical Calderón-Zygmund theory to this refined scale of spaces.

## Behavior of Other Operators

Finally, the paper investigates the behavior of additional classes of operators on the Hardy-Lorentz spaces. Beyond the singular integrals treated in detail, we analyze how various other operators of interest in harmonic analysis interact with the $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ framework. This broader examination underscores the versatility of the atomic and interpolation techniques developed earlier and highlights the utility of the Hardy-Lorentz spaces as a natural setting for operator theory.

## Conclusion

Taken together, the results of this paper provide a comprehensive treatment of the Hardy-Lorentz spaces $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for $0 < p \le 1$ and $0 < q \le \infty$. Through the development of atomic decompositions, the establishment of interpolation properties, and the analysis of singular integrals and other operators, this work contributes both foundational structural insights and practical analytic tools to the theory of these spaces.

# Hardy-Lorentz Spaces: Atomic Decomposition and Operator Theory

## Introduction

The theory of Hardy spaces has played a central role in modern harmonic analysis since its inception, providing a natural framework for studying problems that lie beyond the reach of classical Lebesgue spaces. When the integrability parameter falls in the range $0 < p \le 1$, the classical Lebesgue spaces $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ lose many of their desirable properties—most notably, singular integral operators fail to be bounded on them. The Hardy spaces $H^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ were introduced precisely to remedy this deficiency, serving as appropriate substitutes on which the fundamental operators of analysis behave well.

This paper investigates the **Hardy-Lorentz spaces** $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for the parameter range $0 < p \le 1$ and $0 < q \le \infty$. These spaces arise naturally by replacing the underlying Lebesgue space in the definition of $H^p$ with the finer scale of Lorentz spaces $L^{p,q}$. The Lorentz spaces themselves refine the Lebesgue scale by separating the roles played by the two indices: the parameter $p$ governs the size of a function through its distribution, while the secondary index $q$ provides an additional degree of fine-tuning. The Hardy-Lorentz spaces thus interpolate between and extend the classical Hardy spaces, offering a more delicate instrument for the analysis of functions and distributions.

## Definitions and Preliminaries

Let $\varphi \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ be a fixed Schwartz function with $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi \, dx \neq 0$, and for $t > 0$ write $\varphi_t(x) = t^{-n}\varphi(x/t)$. For a tempered distribution $f \in \mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$, we define the associated **grand maximal function** (or, equivalently, the radial or nontangential maximal function) by
$$
Mf(x) = \sup_{t > 0} |(f * \varphi_t)(x)|.
$$
The Hardy-Lorentz space $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is then defined as the collection of all tempered distributions $f$ for which $Mf$ belongs to the Lorentz space $L^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and we set
$$
\|f\|_{H^{p,q}} = \|Mf\|_{L^{p,q}}.
$$
Here the Lorentz quasi-norm is defined in terms of the decreasing rearrangement $f^*$ of $f$ by
$$
\|f\|_{L^{p,q}} = \left( \int_0^\infty \left( t^{1/p} f^*(t) \right)^q \frac{dt}{t} \right)^{1/q}
$$
for $0 < q < \infty$, with the usual modification $\|f\|_{L^{p,\infty}} = \sup_{t > 0} t^{1/p} f^*(t)$ when $q = \infty$. As in the classical setting, the definition of $H^{p,q}$ can be shown to be independent of the particular choice of the defining function $\varphi$, so that these spaces are intrinsically well-defined.

## Atomic Decomposition

The cornerstone of our analysis is the **atomic decomposition** of the elements of $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. As in the classical Hardy space theory, atoms provide a concrete and manageable set of building blocks from which every element of the space may be reconstructed, and they reduce many analytical questions to verifications on a single, well-understood object.

Recall that, for $0 < p \le 1 \le r \le \infty$ with $r > p$, a function $a$ is called a **$(p,r)$-atom** if it is supported in a cube (or ball) $Q$, satisfies the size condition
$$
\|a\|_{L^r} \le |Q|^{1/r - 1/p},
$$
and possesses the vanishing moment conditions
$$
\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} a(x)\, x^\alpha \, dx = 0 \quad \text{for all multi-indices } |\alpha| \le \left\lfloor n\left(\tfrac{1}{p} - 1\right) \right\rfloor.
$$

The main structural theorem asserts that every $f \in H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ admits a decomposition
$$
f = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \sum_{j} \lambda_{k,j} \, a_{k,j},
$$
where each $a_{k,j}$ is a $(p,r)$-atom associated with a cube $Q_{k,j}$, the coefficients $\lambda_{k,j}$ encode the level sets of the maximal function at scale $2^k$, and the convergence takes place both in $\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and in the quasi-norm of the space. Crucially, the coefficients satisfy a quantitative control expressed through a Lorentz-type sequence quasi-norm that is comparable to $\|f\|_{H^{p,q}}$. Conversely, any series of this form with appropriately controlled coefficients converges to an element of $H^{p,q}$ whose quasi-norm is dominated by the corresponding coefficient quantity.

The proof proceeds through the Calderón-Zygmund decomposition of the distribution $f$ at each dyadic level of its maximal function, followed by careful estimates that track the interaction between the size parameter $p$ and the fine index $q$. The essential subtlety, absent in the classical theory, lies in summing the atomic pieces in a manner compatible with the Lorentz quasi-norm rather than the Lebesgue norm; this requires refined summation arguments that respect the two-parameter structure.

## Interpolation Properties

A significant portion of this work is devoted to the **interpolation properties** of the Hardy-Lorentz spaces. Because the secondary index $q$ arises naturally from the real interpolation method, the family $\{H^{p,q}\}$ enjoys interpolation relations that mirror those of the Lorentz scale. We establish that the Hardy-Lorentz spaces occur precisely as the real interpolation spaces between classical Hardy spaces:
$$
\left( H^{p_0}, H^{p_1} \right)_{\theta, q} = H^{p,q},
$$
where $0 < p_0 < p_1 \le 1$, $0 < \theta < 1$, and $\frac{1}{p} = \frac{1-\theta}{p_0} + \frac{\theta}{p_1}$. This identification exhibits the Hardy-Lorentz spaces as the natural intermediate spaces of the Hardy scale, and it provides a powerful mechanism for transferring results between spaces.

These interpolation theorems have immediate practical consequences: they permit one to deduce the boundedness of operators on $H^{p,q}$ from endpoint estimates on the classical spaces $H^{p_0}$ and $H^{p_1}$. In this way, interpolation and atomic decomposition function as complementary tools, the former offering a global perspective and the latter a local, constructive one.

## Boundedness of Singular Integrals and Other Operators

With the atomic decomposition and interpolation machinery in place, we turn to the **action of operators** on the Hardy-Lorentz spaces. The principal application concerns **Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operators**. Let $T$ be a convolution-type singular integral operator whose kernel satisfies the standard size and smoothness (Hörmander) conditions, together with sufficient cancellation. We prove that $T$ extends to a bounded operator
$$
T : H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n) \longrightarrow H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)
$$
for the full range $0 < p \le 1$ and $0 < q \le \infty$. The strategy is to establish the appropriate uniform estimate on atoms—showing that $T$ maps atoms into fixed multiples of so-called molecules—and then to invoke the atomic decomposition and a summation argument adapted to the Lorentz quasi-norm.

Beyond convolution operators, our methods apply to a broad class of sublinear and linear operators, including the **Riesz transforms**, certain **maximal operators**, and multiplier operators of Hörmander-Mikhlin type. For each such operator, the boundedness on $H^{p,q}$ follows from a combination of atom-level estimates and, where appropriate, interpolation between endpoint bounds. We also record consequences for the boundedness of operators from $H^{p,q}$ into the Lorentz spaces $L^{p,q}$, which recover and refine known results in the classical case $q = p$.

## Conclusion

Taken together, the results of this paper provide a coherent and largely self-contained treatment of the Hardy-Lorentz spaces $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ in the range $0 < p \le 1$, $0 < q \le \infty$. The atomic decomposition furnishes a flexible structural description of the elements of these spaces; the interpolation theorems situate them precisely within the broader landscape of Hardy and Lorentz spaces; and the boundedness results for singular integrals and related operators demonstrate that these spaces retain the essential virtues that make Hardy spaces indispensable in harmonic analysis. By working consistently within the two-parameter Lorentz framework, we obtain a finer and more versatile theory than the classical one, opening the way to sharper endpoint estimates and to further applications in the analysis of partial differential equations and function spaces.

The proofs combine the atomic decomposition with molecular estimates and interpolation, and we deduce corresponding results for Riesz transforms and multiplier operators. Our results unify and extend earlier work on Hardy and Lorentz spaces, providing a self-contained framework for harmonic analysis in the Hardy-Lorentz setting.
